units: the writer answers someone close who was worried about how she was
a change of home came before a stretch of bad sleep
the ringing of the phone made her body clench
an acquaintance suggested she write down her anxieties at the end of the day
she thought the advice absurd before she took it up
the writing brought out a recurring fear of being left behind
a specialist traced that anxious bond back to childhood
she now warns the people close to her instead of shutting herself away
text: Your message asked whether I was any better, so let me go back to where it started. The week we moved, sleep came apart, and every time the phone rang my shoulders locked as though someone had shouted at me. A woman I know told me to write down, each evening, whatever had tightened my throat that day. It struck me as a daft thing to do. I did it anyway. Ten evenings in, the same fear kept turning up on the page: that the people I love would quietly let me go. A psychologist put it plainly. A bond as anxious as that takes shape early, in childhood, and it loosens once you dare ask for help. So now I tell people when I am struggling, instead of disappearing without a word. It still costs me something. Last night I laughed properly, without keeping watch on myself. Write soon, and tell me about your week.

units: a mental health specialist answers questions about thoughts that keep repeating
the brain meets a threat to a relationship almost as it meets a threat to the body
the scene is replayed in the hope of finding a way out
the repeating holds the alarm open instead of settling it
the open alarm sets the repeating thoughts going again
sleep is broken because the watch kept inside does not stop at night
those close by tire of hearing the same complaint and draw away
that withdrawal deepens the loneliness of the one who ruminates
the specialist advises writing the whole episode out once
text: What becomes of a grievance you cannot put down? We put the question to a researcher in clinical psychology. Her answer came in a single word: rumination. A threat to a relationship registers in the brain much as a threat to the body does, and so the scene is replayed, again and again, in the hope that some way out will show itself. Does the replaying help? Not at all. It holds the alarm open, and the open alarm sets the thoughts running once more. Why is the sleep of such people broken? Because the watch kept inside never stands down when the light goes off. And those around them? They tire of the same complaint and drift away, which leaves the one who ruminates lonelier than before. What, then, does she advise? Writing the episode out whole, one evening, from end to end, and shutting the notebook. Thoughts given sentences stop circling.

units: a young girl admits she cannot put what she feels into words
her aunt does not press her and pours her something hot to drink
the aunt says she kept quiet at the same age out of reserve
the aunt holds that such silence shuts you in rather than shields you
the girl is afraid her words would set her mother crying
the aunt suggests placing the sensation instead of naming the sorrow
the girl points to two spots on her neck
her breathing loosens once she has described them
they settle on a hand laid on the table as an agreed signal
the mother sits down beside her without asking a thing
text: I cannot say what I feel, the girl murmured, her eyes on the rug. Her aunt did not press her. She poured out tea, and admitted that at the same age she had kept quiet too, out of a kind of reserve. You believe you are sparing everyone, she said, and all you do is shut yourself in. The girl answered that words felt too heavy, and that hers would set her mother crying. So her aunt offered a way round it: describe not the sorrow but the place where it sits. The throat first, the girl said, then the back of the neck, and her breathing loosened as she said it. They settled on a signal, hardly visible to anyone else: a hand laid flat on the table would mean it was time to talk. That evening the hand went down, and her mother came and sat beside her, asking nothing at all. The wordless thing calmed the whole house.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: having no instruments, the old practitioners went by what patients told them
their approach joined long listening to the setting side by side of similar cases
practitioners who came later took bodily measurements
among those measurements were the beat of the heart and the length of sleep
the old approach caught the fine shading but missed the regularities
the instrumented approach caught the regularities but lost the fine shading
a feeling pushed out of awareness produces no sign that can be measured
the two approaches were later joined together
each makes up for the blind spot of the other
text: Before recording instruments existed, physicians described disorders of mood from what their patients told them, and nothing else. The method rested on listening at length and on setting like cases beside one another. Clinicians trained later went about it differently: they measured the beat of the heart, the resistance of the skin, the hours of sleep. The older way caught the fine shading and missed the regularities; the instrumented one caught the regularities and let the shading escape. The difference lies in the material itself, for a feeling pushed out of awareness leaves no mark a device can pick up, whereas a bodily reaction writes itself down. In the end the two traditions met: the patient is questioned while his inner responses are followed, and the records compared afterwards. Neither replaces the other, and each corrects the blind spot of its neighbour.

units: three sorts of sign reveal that the person you are talking to is uneasy
the first sign is a matter of posture, with the shoulders drawing in
a hand travelling up towards the face goes with that posture
the second sign is in the voice, whose pace slackens
the third sign belongs to the eyes, which settle on nothing
unease has to do with the picture one gives to others
fear, on the contrary, has to do with a danger coming from outside
shame is set apart by lasting longer and cutting deeper
an alert onlooker can lower his voice and look away
text: Three sorts of sign will tell you that the person in front of you is uneasy. The first is a matter of posture: the shoulders draw in, the chin drops, and a hand travels up towards the face as though to cover it. The second lies in the voice, where the pace slackens, sentences break off, and the tone loses its footing. The third belongs to the eyes, which slide away, come back briefly, and settle on nothing. What separates these signals from those of fear is their target, since unease has to do with the picture one gives to others, while fear has to do with a danger coming from outside. They differ from shame as well, which lasts longer and cuts deeper, and drives a person to withdraw altogether. Reading them is of most use to the onlooker, who can lower his voice, look away, leave a gap in the talk. That restraint often makes the conversation bearable for the one who feels exposed.

units: a singer who is not a professional attends an audition in a borrowed hall
he had worked at his piece for several weeks
an uneasiness took hold of him the moment he stepped onto the platform
his hands went cold and his voice missed the opening
the panel granted him a second try
that second attempt turned out worse than the first
a woman musician suggested he stand with his back to the room
the performance then came out true and easy
he afterwards sang the ending again facing the room
he puts his trouble down to being looked at and not to the singing
text: A singer who does not do it for a living came to an audition in a hall lent by a group of musicians. He had worked at his piece for weeks and believed himself ready. The moment he stepped onto the platform something turned over in him: the ceiling seemed to come down, his hands went cold, and his voice missed the opening note. He asked to begin again, and the panel let him. The second attempt was worse than the first. One of the accompanists then suggested he sing with his back to the room. He laughed, and tried it. The piece came out whole, in tune, almost easy. They asked him afterwards to turn round and take the last verse facing them, and he sang it without a tremor. What frightened him, he decided, was never the singing but the being looked at, and the smallest detour had been enough to disarm it.

units: the first step is to spot the bodily signal of anxiety
naming the feeling with a word takes some of its force away
you must write down exactly the outcome you dread
you then weigh the gravity you imagine against how likely it really is
lengthening the outward breath slows the beat of the heart
arriving early spares you the strain of a room already filled
putting your feet on the floor tells the brain where the body's balance is
asking for a drink breaks the runaway feeling if panic comes
text: Start by catching the moment your stomach tightens before a meeting, because a feeling that has been named loses some of its force. Then put down in your notebook exactly what you dread: being cut off, coming across as useless, sitting through an awkward silence. Write the outcome you picture, and beside it how likely it really is, and the gap between the two will jump out at you. Breathe afterwards, drawing the outward breath long, since it is the going out and not the coming in that steadies the beat of the heart. Arrive a little early, because walking into a room already filled winds you up, whereas taking your seat before the others lets it drop. While the talk goes on, keep both feet flat on the floor, as that contact tells the brain where your balance is. And if panic climbs all the same, ask for water: the gesture gives you something to hold and breaks the loop.

units: a place offering psychological support opened in a street of shops
the men who were seen there lost their temper in the first session
those men did not turn up for the sessions that followed
the team first put those departures down to a want of willingness
the reception room could be seen from the street through a pane of glass
being open to view turned unease into aggression
the entrance was moved round to the courtyard side
a curtain was hung and the lighting brought down
the number of people breaking off their treatment fell by half
the manager advises studying the place before explaining a behaviour
text: In an old quarter, a counselling centre opened at the end of a street of small shops. The staff kept meeting the same wall: men who came to be seen lost their temper in the first session, and then never appeared again. The team put it at first down to a want of willingness. Closer observation showed something else. The reception room was glazed onto the street, so that whoever sat there sat in full view of the people going past, and the unease turned into aggression. The remedy was a matter of building work before it was a matter of therapy. The entrance was moved round to the inner courtyard, a heavy curtain was hung, the lighting was brought down. Within a season, the number of people breaking off after the first appointment had fallen by half. The manager draws a lesson from it that she repeats to her trainees: before you explain a behaviour, look hard at the place that produced it.

units: a waiting room stands apart from the other spaces in the building
its walls are a muted green against a corridor of glaring white
the seats there are turned towards one another
in the corridor the seats are ranged along the wall
a thick floor covering smothers the sound of footsteps
the hard floor of the entrance, on the contrary, throws the noise back
worn magazines lie on a low piece of furniture
those who arrive show a keen agitation in voice and gesture
they leave the room at a steadier pace
text: The waiting room at the practice is like no other space in the building. Its walls carry a muted green, where the corridor next door is a glare of white. In here the armchairs are turned slightly towards one another, as though a conversation were expected; out there the chairs are ranged along the partition. A thick carpet swallows the sound of footsteps, while the tiled floor of the entrance throws every heel back at you. On the low table lie worn magazines, shabbier than the ones at the desk, and perhaps it is that untidiness which reassures. The people who come in are keyed up, their voices pitched high, their hands quick; they go out again at a steadier pace, the jaw unclenched. The room cures nothing, of course. It only prepares, the way an airlock does, the passage from one inward state to another.

units: the writer disputes the idea that sadness is a fault to be put right
a feeling points to what has value for the one who feels it
the pace of exchanges on screens makes a mood that lasts look suspect
that pressure leads people to dread their own inward slowness
the ways of assessing things favour whatever can be counted
inward experience therefore falls outside the studies, for want of any way to code it
a feeling pushed down comes back as irritability or exhaustion
the writer grants that pain which goes on belongs to proper care
treating ordinary sorrow as an illness takes from each of us the words to speak of ourselves
text: We ought to stop treating sadness as a fault to be put right. First point: a feeling is not a defect of manufacture, it is information about what has value for the one who feels it. Second point: the pace demanded by our exchanges on screens makes any mood that lasts look suspect, so that we end by dreading our own inward slowness. Third point: the ways we have of assessing things favour whatever can be counted, and inward experience, being hard to code, drops out of the studies. Fourth point: a feeling pushed down does not go away, it comes back elsewhere, as irritability or as a tiredness that will not lift. Someone will object that pain which goes on and on belongs to proper care, and the objection holds. But to run ordinary sorrow together with illness is to take from each of us the words for saying what we are living through.
